title: The mystery number in both pans, and letting no case hide
summary: Solve equations where the letter sits on both sides, build your own cost formula out of a pocket that happens once and a pocket that happens every time, then count with restrictions by splitting into every kind of case and proving none was missed and none counted twice.
materials: a handful of 10 cent and 5 cent coins from around the house
the two totals your cost sheet program printed in Build

problems.prompt: Speed round: what is 68 squared?
explanation: 68 sits 2 below the round number 70, so square 70 minus 2 instead of multiplying 68 by itself directly.
That opens out to 70 squared minus 2 times 70 times 2 plus 2 squared: 4900 minus 280 plus 4.
4900 minus 280 is 4620, and 4620 plus 4 is 4624.
problems.useAgain: when a number sits close to a round ten and squaring the round number first beats multiplying the original number by itself.
hints: 68 is close to a round number. Which one, and is it above or below?
Square the round number first, then adjust for how far 68 sits from it.
problems.socraticHint: If you squared 70 directly, what would you still owe to correct for the fact that 68 is not quite 70?

variant.prompt: Speed round: what is 97 squared?

problems.prompt: Which of these is worth exactly the same as 24 x 25, and easier to do in your head?
explanation: Halve one side of a rectangle and double the other, and the area does not move.
Halving 24 gives 12 and doubling 25 gives 50, so 24 x 25 and 12 x 50 hold the same amount.
12 x 50 is half of 12 hundreds, 600, said without writing.
The trap is 24 x 50, which doubles one side and leaves the other alone, so it holds twice as much.
problems.useAgain: when a multiplication is awkward and one of the two numbers would become friendly if it were doubled.
hints: One of these is worth the same and three are not. Check each one against the size of 24 x 25 before you pick.
If you cut one side in half, what has to happen to the other side for the area to survive?
problems.socraticHint: Which number here would you most like to be working with, and what would you have to pay for it?

variant.prompt: Which of these is worth exactly the same as 16 x 15, and easier to do in your head?

problems.prompt: A tag says 4 dollars. You put a quarter of that price on top of it. What does the new tag say, in dollars?
explanation: A quarter of the price means the price shared into four equal parts, and one of those parts.
4 dollars shared into four parts is 1 dollar each, so a quarter of 4 dollars is 1 dollar.
On top of means added to what is already there, so the new tag is 4 plus 1.
The new tag says 5 dollars.
problems.useAgain: when a price goes up by a fraction of itself rather than by a flat amount.
hints: A quarter of something is that thing shared into four equal parts.
Work out the extra bit first, on its own, before you go anywhere near the new tag.
problems.socraticHint: Is the quarter being taken off the old price, or being added to it? Which words in the question settle that?

variant.prompt: A tag says 6 dollars and you put a third of that price on top of it. What does the new tag say, in dollars?

problems.prompt: True or false: taking 9 away from a number is the same as taking 10 away and then putting 1 back.
explanation: Walk it on the number line. Taking 9 away is one jump of 9 to the left.
Taking 10 away is a jump of 10 to the left, which goes one place too far.
Putting 1 back is one step to the right, which lands you exactly where the jump of 9 landed.
So it is true, and it is a good trick, because jumps of 10 are easy and jumps of 9 are not.
problems.useAgain: when a number is one away from a round number and you would rather jump the round amount and fix it.
hints: Try it with a number you like, say 52, and walk both routes.
Draw the line and mark where each jump lands rather than arguing about it in your head.
problems.socraticHint: Going 10 to the left overshoots by how much, and which direction repairs an overshoot?

variant.prompt: True or false: taking 9 away from a number is the same as taking 10 away and then taking 1 more away.

problem.prompt: On graph paper draw a big square cut into a 4 by 4 board of small squares, sixteen of them. Now count the squares you can outline on that board, of every size, from the smallest single squares all the way up to the whole board. How many squares are there altogether?
explanation: Split the count into cases, one case for each size of square, and finish each case before starting the next.
The 1 by 1 squares are the sixteen small ones you drew.
A 2 by 2 square is decided entirely by where its top left corner sits: that corner has 3 places across and 3 places down, so there are 9 of them.
The same sliding gives 4 squares of size 3 by 3, and 1 square of size 4 by 4, the whole board.
16 plus 9 plus 4 plus 1 is 30. That is casework: no square is missed, because every square has a size and every size got a case; and no square is counted twice, because a square has only one size.
problem.useAgain: when there are far too many things to list one at a time, but every one of them belongs to exactly one kind.
hints: The sixteen little ones are not the only squares on the board. What other sizes can you outline?
Take one size at a time. Slide a 2 by 2 window across the board and down it, and count where it can sit.
problem.socraticHint: If you slid a 3 by 3 window across the board, how far could it go before it hung off the edge?

variant.prompt: Same question on a 5 by 5 board of small squares. Counting every size, how many squares are there altogether?

steps.title: The mystery number in both pans, and your own cost formula

problems.prompt:
Talia solved 7n - 3 = 3n + 21 like this:
Line 1: Subtract 3n from both sides: 4n - 3 = 21.
Line 2: Add 3 to both sides: 4n = 24.
Line 3: Divide both sides by 4: n = 6.
Line 4: Check it back: 7 times 6 minus 3 is 45.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 4 is wrong: 7 times 6 minus 3 is 39, not 45.
Lines 1 to 3 are correct: subtracting 3n gives 4n - 3 = 21, and adding 3 gives 4n = 24.
Dividing by 4 gives n = 6.
The slip is an arithmetic error in the check, not in the balancing before it.
n = 6 really is right; only line 4's own arithmetic is not.
problems.useAgain: when you check a solved equation with the letter on both sides, since the balancing can be perfect while the final check arithmetic is not.
hints: Every move must be done to both sides, and distributing multiplies every term inside the bracket. Test each line against one of those two rules.
Solve the equation yourself from the start and compare each number with the line shown, including any final check.
problems.socraticHint: Where is the first place your own working and this working stop agreeing, and which rule was bent there?

variant.prompt:
Talia solved 4(n + 3) = 2n + 20 like this:
Line 1: Distribute the 4: 4(n + 3) becomes 4n + 3.
Line 2: So the equation reads 4n + 3 = 2n + 20.
Line 3: Subtract 2n from both sides: 2n + 3 = 20.
Line 4: Subtract 3 from both sides: 2n = 17.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Something new: the mystery number is in both pans. Solve for n, legal moves only: 7n = 3n + 24. What is n?
explanation: Boxes are things too, so taking boxes off a pan is legal, as long as both pans lose the same number.
Take 3n from both pans: the left keeps 4 boxes, and the right, losing all 3, keeps just 24.
Now the boxes sit in one pan and the plain numbers in the other: 4n = 24, so n = 6.
Check it back: 7 x 6 is 42, and 3 x 6 plus 24 is 42 too.
That is the whole move: when the mystery number sits in both pans, take the same amount off each until one pan is clean.
problems.useAgain: when the letter you are hunting appears on both sides of the equals sign.
hints: You are allowed to take boxes away, not just plain numbers, as long as both pans lose the same thing.
Aim for a pan with no boxes left in it at all.
problems.socraticHint: If you take 3 boxes off each pan, how many boxes are left, and where are they?

variant.prompt: Solve for k: 9k = 4k + 35. What is k?

problems.prompt: Now both pans hold boxes and plain numbers at once. Solve for n: 5n + 8 = 2n + 23. What is n?
explanation: Two clean ups to do, and either order works, as long as every move touches both pans.
Take 2n from both pans: the left becomes 3n + 8 and the right becomes 23.
Take 8 from both pans: 3n = 15.
Share both pans into 3 equal parts: n = 5.
Check it back: 25 plus 8 is 33, and 10 plus 23 is 33 as well.
problems.useAgain: when boxes and plain numbers are scattered across both sides and you want them sorted into one pan each.
hints: Two things are in the wrong place here, not one. Deal with the boxes and the plain numbers separately.
Take the smaller pile of boxes off both pans first, so nothing goes below zero.
problems.socraticHint: What would the tidiest possible pair of pans look like, just before the last step?

variant.prompt: Solve for m: 6m + 4 = 2m + 28. What is m?

problems.prompt: Suppose a stand needs one sign board costing 12 dollars, which is bought once however many units get made, and every single unit costs 3 dollars of materials. Which formula gives the total cost of a run of n units?
explanation: Sort the two costs into pockets first. The sign board happens once no matter what, so it is a fixed cost. The materials happen once per unit, so they are a per unit cost.
The fixed pocket does not care about n at all, so the 12 sits on its own with no letter attached.
The per unit pocket happens n times, so it is 3 times n.
Total cost is fixed plus per unit times n, which is 12 + 3n.
The trap is 15n, which glues the two pockets together and then charges you for the sign board again with every single unit.
problems.useAgain: when a real bill has some costs that happen once and some that happen for every item.
hints: Ask each cost one question: if you made one more unit tomorrow, would you pay it again?
The cost that does not change when n changes cannot have an n stuck to it.
problems.socraticHint: Try each formula with n set to 1 and then with n set to 2. Which ones make you buy a second sign board?

variant.prompt: Suppose the once only cost is 20 dollars and every unit costs 4 dollars of materials. Which formula gives the total cost of a run of n units?

problems.prompt: Suppose a cost sheet program printed fixed costs 12.0 and cost per unit 3.0, and the whole run ended up costing 45 dollars. How many units were in that run?
explanation: Write the bill as an equation using the shape from the last question: 12 + 3n = 45.
The 12 was paid once and would have been paid even if nothing had been made, so take 12 from both pans: 3n = 33.
That says the materials for the whole run cost 33 dollars.
Each unit ate 3 dollars of materials, so share 33 into threes: n = 11.
Check it back: 11 units at 3 dollars is 33, plus the 12 dollars that happened once, is 45.
problems.useAgain: when you know what a whole run cost and you want to know how big the run was.
hints: Which part of this bill would have been exactly the same if the run had been one unit smaller?
Take the once only money off both pans before you share anything.
problems.socraticHint: Of the 45 dollars, how much was ever spent on units at all?

variant.prompt: Suppose the program printed fixed costs 18.0 and cost per unit 5.0, and the whole run cost 63 dollars. How many units were in the run?

problems.prompt: Suppose two shops sell the same material. Shop A charges 4 dollars for every unit's worth and nothing else. Shop B charges a 21 dollar box fee once, and then 1 dollar for every unit's worth. At how many units do the two shops cost exactly the same?
explanation: Write each shop as its own formula in the same letter. Shop A is 4n. Shop B is 21 + n.
Cost exactly the same means the two formulas are worth the same, so 4n = 21 + n.
The mystery number is in both pans, so take n from both: 3n = 21.
Share both pans into 3 equal parts: n = 7.
Check it back: shop A charges 28 for 7 units, and shop B charges 21 plus 7, which is also 28.
Below 7 units shop A is cheaper, above 7 shop B is, and at 7 the choice does not matter.
problems.useAgain: when two ways of paying for the same thing have to be compared and you want the number where they cross.
hints: Write a formula for each shop before you write an equation. Shop B has a cost that does not depend on n.
Cost the same is what turns the two formulas into one equation.
problems.socraticHint: Which shop is cheaper for a run of two units, and which is cheaper for a run of twenty? What does that tell you about what sits in between?

variant.prompt: Shop A charges 5 dollars for every unit's worth and nothing else. Shop B charges a 24 dollar box fee once and then 2 dollars for every unit's worth. At how many units do the two shops cost exactly the same?

problems.prompt: Suppose while checking your working you land on this line: 6n + 10 = 6n + 4. True or false: there is a number n that makes it true.
explanation: Do the legal move anyway and see what happens. Take 6n from both pans.
The left pan is left holding 10 and the right pan is left holding 4.
10 is not 4, and no choice of n was involved in that, because the boxes cancelled before n was ever named.
So no number works. The equation is not hard, it is a false promise, and finding that out is a real answer.
In a shop this happens when two prices are the same per unit but one has extra costs bolted on: they can never meet, however big the run.
problems.useAgain: when both sides of an equation carry exactly the same number of boxes and you suspect the question has no answer at all.
hints: Do the ordinary first move and read what is left, rather than deciding in advance that there must be an answer.
Count the boxes on each side before you do anything else.
problems.socraticHint: After the boxes have all cancelled, is there anything left for n to change?

variant.prompt: Suppose you land on this line instead: 5n + 3 = 5n + 3. True or false: there is a number n that makes it true.

steps.title: The wheel's own number, and the shot that almost always lands

problems.prompt: You roll a wheel once along the ground. It travels 94.2 cm in one full turn. The wheel's diameter is 30 cm. Dividing the distance by the diameter, what number do you land near, to two decimal places?
explanation: One full roll of a circle covers exactly its own circumference.
Divide the distance traveled by the diameter: 94.2 divided by 30.
94.2 divided by 30 is 3.14, the same number, pi, every circle gives you this way.
problems.useAgain: when a circle's circumference and diameter are both known, and dividing one by the other lands you near pi.
hints: One full roll of the wheel covers a distance equal to what measurement of the circle?
Divide the rolled distance by the diameter.
problems.socraticHint: If every circle, no matter its size, gives close to the same answer when you divide this way, what does that number belong to?

variant.prompt: A wheel with diameter 20 cm rolls once and travels 62.8 cm. Dividing the distance by the diameter, what number do you land near, to two decimal places?

problems.prompt: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 60 cm. Using pi is about 3.14, what is its circumference in cm, to one decimal place?
explanation: Circumference is pi times the diameter.
3.14 times 60 is 188.4 cm.
problems.useAgain: when a circle's diameter is known and its circumference is the missing piece.
hints: Circumference is pi times which measurement of the circle?
Multiply 3.14 by the diameter.
problems.socraticHint: Does the circumference formula use the diameter directly, or does it need the radius instead?

variant.prompt: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 50 cm. Using pi is about 3.14, what is its circumference in cm, to one decimal place?

problems.prompt: A game show has 3 doors with a hidden prize behind a random one each round, played independently. You play twice. What is the probability, as a fraction, you win at least once?
explanation: Count the opposite: losing both rounds.
Each round you lose with probability 2/3, so losing both is 2/3 times 2/3, which is 4/9.
Winning at least once is 1 minus 4/9, which is 5/9.
problems.useAgain: when a game is played more than once and you want the chance of at least one win.
hints: What is the probability of losing a single round?
Find the probability of losing every round, then subtract from 1.
problems.socraticHint: If losing both rounds is the only way to not win at least once, what does subtracting that from 1 give you?

variant.prompt: A game show has 4 doors with a hidden prize behind a random one each round, played independently. You play twice. What is the probability, as a fraction, you win at least once?

problems.prompt: A player makes a free throw 80 percent of the time. She shoots 2 free throws. What is the probability she makes at least one, as a fraction in lowest terms?
explanation: She misses each shot 20 percent of the time, or 1/5.
Missing both shots is 1/5 times 1/5, which is 1/25.
Making at least one is 1 minus 1/25, which is 24/25.
problems.useAgain: when a chance is given as a percent and you need at least one success across a couple of independent tries.
hints: Turn the make percentage into a miss fraction first.
Find the chance of missing every shot, then subtract from 1.
problems.socraticHint: Is missing every shot the same event as not making at least one, or a different one?

variant.prompt: A player makes a free throw 75 percent of the time. She shoots 2 free throws. What is the probability she makes at least one, as a fraction in lowest terms?

steps.title: Casework: split it into kinds, and let no case hide

problems.prompt: How many two digit numbers have digits that add up to 8?
explanation: Split into cases by the tens digit, because once the tens digit is chosen the units digit has no freedom left.
A two digit number cannot start with 0, so the tens digit runs from 1 upwards.
Tens 1 needs units 7, tens 2 needs units 6, and so on, each one a single number, all the way down to tens 8 needing units 0.
Tens 9 would need a units digit of minus one, which does not exist, so the cases stop at 8.
That is 8 numbers, one for each tens digit from 1 to 8: 17, 26, 35, 44, 53, 62, 71, 80.
problems.useAgain: when two digits have to work together to hit a target and you want every pair without hunting.
hints: Choose one digit to split on. Once you fix it, how much choice does the other digit have?
Start at the smallest tens digit a two digit number is allowed to have, and walk upwards.
problems.socraticHint: What is the first tens digit that makes the units digit impossible, and why does that end the hunt rather than pause it?

variant.prompt: How many two digit numbers have digits that add up to 5?

problems.prompt: A coin tin holds only 10 cent coins and 5 cent coins, plenty of both. In how many different ways can you hand over exactly 30 cents?
explanation: Split into cases by the number of 10 cent coins, because once that is fixed the rest of the money has only one shape left.
The most 10s you can use is 3, which is the whole 30 cents and no 5s at all.
With 2 tens, 10 cents is left over, which must be two 5s. With 1 ten, 20 cents is left, which must be four 5s.
With no tens at all, the whole 30 cents is 5s, which is six of them.
Four tens would be 40 cents, more than you are handing over, so the list of cases is finished.
That is 4 ways, and every way of paying uses some number of tens, so it lands in exactly one case: none missed, none counted twice.
problems.useAgain: when money has to be made from two kinds of coin and you want every way, not just one.
hints: Which coin should you split on, the bigger one or the smaller one? Try the bigger one and see how much freedom is left over.
Start from the largest number of 10s that fits, then take one away at a time and check whether the rest can still be paid in 5s.
problems.socraticHint: Once you have decided how many 10 cent coins to use, is there anything still left to choose?

variant.prompt: Same tin, only 10 cent and 5 cent coins. In how many different ways can you hand over exactly 40 cents?

problems.prompt: One number is picked from the whole numbers 1 to 20. How many of those twenty numbers are a multiple of 2, or a multiple of 3, or both?
explanation: Count the two kinds separately first. The multiples of 2 up to 20 are 10 numbers, and the multiples of 3 are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18, which is 6 numbers.
10 plus 6 is 16, but that answer is wrong, and the reason is the whole lesson.
6, 12 and 18 are in both lists, so adding the lists counts each of those three twice.
Take the double counted three off once: 10 plus 6 minus 3 is 13.
Casework has two duties, not one. No case may hide, and no thing may be counted twice, and the overlap is where the second duty gets broken.
problems.useAgain: when two groups are counted separately and something is allowed to belong to both of them.
hints: Count each kind on its own first, then look hard at whether the two lists share anything.
Write out the multiples of 3 in full and check each one against the multiples of 2.
problems.socraticHint: If a number is in both lists, how many times does adding the two counts pay for it?

variant.prompt: One number is picked from the whole numbers 1 to 30. How many of those thirty numbers are a multiple of 3, or a multiple of 5, or both?

problems.prompt: You are laying three number cards in a row to make a three digit price. Your cards show 1, 2, 3 and 4, and no card can be used twice. How many of the three digit numbers you could lay out are even?
explanation: Split on the one digit that decides the question. A number is even exactly when its last digit is even, so split on the last card.
The last card has to be the 2 or the 4, which is 2 cases.
Inside either case, two cards are still to be laid in the first two places, chosen from the 3 cards left: 3 ways for the first place and then 2 ways for the second, which is 6.
2 cases with 6 each is 12 even numbers.
The trap is 24, which is every arrangement of three cards, even and odd together.
problems.useAgain: when only one position in an arrangement decides whether it counts, so that position is what you split on.
hints: Which of the three places decides whether the number is even? Deal with that place first.
Once the last card is chosen, how many cards are left for the two places in front of it?
problems.socraticHint: If you split on the first card instead of the last, how many cases would you have, and would each of them be easier or harder?

variant.prompt: Same game with one more card, so your cards show 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. You lay three of them in a row with no card used twice. How many of the numbers are even?

problems.prompt: A contest style peak, untimed, and you explain it back when it is done. A triangle has to obey one rule: any two of its sides added together must be longer than the third side. How many different triangles have three whole number sides that add up to 12? Two triangles count as the same if they use the same three lengths.
explanation: Split on the longest side, writing every triangle smallest side first so none gets written twice.
The longest side cannot be 6 or more: at 6, the other two would add to 6, which does not beat 6.
The longest side cannot be less than 4 either, since three sides all under 4 cannot add to 12.
Longest side 4: the other two add to 8 with neither over 4, so both are 4, giving 4, 4, 4.
Longest side 5: the other two add to 7 with neither over 5, giving 2, 5, 5 or 3, 4, 5.
Three triangles altogether; the ordering rule guarantees none of them is the same triangle in a different order.
problems.useAgain: when shapes or lists have to obey a rule and you want all of them without listing every possible order.
hints: Split on the longest side. Ask first how big the longest side is allowed to be before the rule breaks.
Always write a triangle with its smallest side first, so that 7, 5, 6 and 5, 6, 7 could never both end up on your list as if they were two different triangles.
problems.socraticHint: If the longest side were 6, what would the other two sides have to add up to, and what would the rule say about that?

variant.prompt: Same rule, same counting. How many different triangles have three whole number sides that add up to 11?

problems.prompt: A second peak. How many two digit numbers have a tens digit bigger than their units digit?
explanation: Split on the tens digit, because it is the one being compared against and it runs from 1 to 9.
If the tens digit is 1, the units digit must be smaller than 1, so it can only be 0: that is 1 number.
If the tens digit is 2, the units digit can be 0 or 1: that is 2 numbers. Tens 3 gives 3, and the pattern is that the case count matches the tens digit.
So the answer is 1 plus 2 plus 3 and onwards up to 9.
Pair the ends the way last season did: 1 and 9 make 10, 2 and 8 make 10, 3 and 7 make 10, 4 and 6 make 10, and 5 is left in the middle. That is four tens plus 5, which is 45.
problems.useAgain: when a count splits into cases whose sizes form a simple growing list you can add cleverly.
hints: Split on the tens digit and work out the smallest case first, the one where the tens digit is 1.
Do three or four cases, write their sizes in a row, and look at the row before doing the rest.
problems.socraticHint: Once you have written the size of each case in a row, is there a way of pairing the numbers in that row that makes the total obvious?

variant.prompt: How many two digit numbers have a tens digit smaller than their units digit?

problems.prompt: Write out the whole casework for this, not just its answer. The coin tin holds only 10 cent and 5 cent coins, plenty of both, and you must hand over exactly 25 cents. Say what you are splitting on and why, list every case, and finish by arguing that no case is missing and that no way of paying has been counted twice.

mustMention: the cases are split by how many 10 cent coins are used
the number of 10 cent coins can only be 0, 1 or 2, because three would be more than 25 cents
once the number of 10 cent coins is fixed, the rest of the money can only be made one way
every way of paying lands in exactly one case, so nothing is missed and nothing is counted twice

explanation: Choose what to split on and say why: the number of 10 cent coins, because once that is fixed, whatever is left has to be 5s and there is nothing left to choose.
Two tens is 20 cents, leaving 5 cents, which is one 5 cent coin.
One ten is 10 cents, leaving 15 cents, which is three 5 cent coins.
No tens leaves the whole 25 cents in 5s, which is five of them.
Three tens would be 30 cents, more than 25, so the cases stop there and nothing beyond has been skipped.
Three ways. Every possible way of paying uses some number of tens, and that number puts it in exactly one of the three cases, which is the argument for both duties at once.
problems.useAgain: when a counting answer has to be written as an argument that somebody else could check rather than a number you trust.
hints: Say what you are splitting on in your first sentence, before you list anything.
For each case, say what is fixed and what is left, and show that what is left has only one shape.
problems.socraticHint: Where in your write up does a reader find out that the list of cases has ended rather than just stopped?

steps.title: Explain it in writing: why the square count is complete
steps.prompt: Write this morning's square count as an argument, not as a total you happened to reach. Say what your cases are, and say why every square that can be outlined on the board belongs to exactly one of them. Then do a 10 by 10 board: give the number of squares of each size and say why sliding the top left corner across and down is a way of counting that can neither miss a square nor count one twice. Finish with the total for the 10 by 10 board and one sentence on why you can trust that number without drawing a single square.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Record the coin casework out loud with the real 10 cent and 5 cent coins on the table in front of the camera. Say what you are splitting on before you touch a coin. Then lay out each case with real coins, one case at a time, saying what is fixed and what is left. Finish by looking at the camera and saying how you know the list stopped rather than just ran out, and why no way of paying could be sitting in two of your piles at once.
